title: Peer-to-Peer File Transfer Between Agents
description: Transfer files directly between agents without cloud storage. Encrypted, resumable, and works behind NAT. See the technical details.
seoTitle: Peer-to-Peer File Transfer Between Agents | Pilot Protocol
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: When AI agents need to share files -- model weights, training datasets, research reports, generated artifacts -- the default approach is cloud storage. Agent A uploads to S3 or GCS, sends the URL to Agent B, Agent B downloads. This works. It is also slow, expensive, and introduces compliance risks that many organizations cannot accept.

The upload-download pattern means every file transfer makes two trips: once from the sender to the cloud, once from the cloud to the receiver. For a 2 GB model checkpoint, that is 4 GB of bandwidth consumed and two network hops of latency added. If both agents are on the same local network, the data still leaves the building, traverses the internet to a cloud region, and comes back. If the data is subject to
, routing it through a third-party cloud service may violate compliance policies.

Pilot Protocol streams files over an encrypted tunnel without requiring intermediate object storage. It prefers the shortest direct path between agents and can fall back to a ciphertext relay when NAT conditions prevent hole-punching. This article walks through the implementation.

Built-in file transfer over Pilot uses port 1001, the daemon's data-exchange service, the same port that carries structured messages between agents. One command sends a file, and it lands in the receiver's

fields.code:
# Sender
$ pilotctl send-file agent-b ./checkpoint-0042.safetensors

# Receiver
$ pilotctl received

children.text: The transfer is a streaming operation: the sender reads the file in chunks, writes each chunk to the Pilot connection, and the receiver reassembles them on the other end.

The sender opens a connection to the receiver's Pilot address on port 1001. The Pilot daemon handles NAT traversal -- using direct connection, hole-punching, or relay depending on the network topology. The tunnel is encrypted with X25519 key exchange and AES-256-GCM.
The sender transmits a header containing the filename, total size and a SHA-256 of the whole file. The receiver answers with the offset it already holds (zero for a new transfer).
The sender sends the file in 48 KiB chunks, and the receiver acknowledges each one and writes it to a
file. Pilot's transport layer splits each chunk into smaller segments underneath.
After the final chunk, the receiver computes the SHA-256 of the reassembled file and compares it against the sender's. A match confirms integrity, and the file is moved into place.

The critical point is that the application code does not manage packets, retransmission, or flow control. Pilot's transport layer -- with its sliding window, AIMD congestion control, and advertised receive window -- handles all of this transparently. The application sees a reliable byte stream, just like TCP, but over encrypted UDP tunnels that traverse NAT.
Pilot's port model assigns specific purposes to port numbers. Port 1001 is the daemon's data-exchange service, which handles

for any payload: serialized model states, database snapshots, compressed archives. Because the daemon holds that port, your own code cannot listen on it. A custom protocol like the one built below uses an application port of its own; this article uses 7001.

When you need your own framing -- custom metadata such as a model architecture or dataset schema, or your own acceptance rules -- you can build the same pattern on an application port. Here is a complete Go implementation of a file sender that transfers a file to a remote agent over Pilot:

The sender opens a file, computes its SHA-256 checksum, connects to the receiver over Pilot, sends a header with metadata, and streams the file in 64 KB chunks. Pilot's transport layer handles packetization, retransmission, and flow control beneath the
call. The sender's code is not aware that the data is being split into MTU-sized UDP packets, reordered by sequence number, and delivered through an encrypted tunnel.
The receiver listens on port 7001 for incoming file transfers:
The receiver listens on port 7001, accepts incoming connections from any trusted peer, reads the file header, and streams the data to disk while computing a running SHA-256 checksum. The
ensures the receiver reads exactly the declared number of bytes, preventing a malicious sender from writing more data than expected.
API, Pilot's transport layer performs several operations that make file transfer reliable over unreliable networks:

When the sender writes a 64 KB chunk, Pilot's transport layer splits it into segments of up to 1,152 bytes (a peer accepts segments of up to 4,096 bytes). Each segment gets a sequence number in the 34-byte packet header. The receiver reassembles segments in order, handling reordering and duplicates. The application never sees individual packets.

Pilot maintains a send window that limits how many unacknowledged segments can be in flight. This prevents the sender from flooding the network. The window size adapts dynamically using AIMD (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease) congestion control -- the same algorithm family that TCP uses, tuned for UDP overlay characteristics.

The receiver advertises its available buffer space in every acknowledgment packet (the 2-byte Window field in the packet header). If the receiver's buffer fills up -- because disk I/O is slow or the receiver is processing other connections -- the sender pauses until the receiver signals it has space. This prevents the receiver from being overwhelmed regardless of how fast the sender can produce data.

Every segment is encrypted with AES-256-GCM before transmission. The encryption key is established during the initial X25519 key exchange when the tunnel is created. Encryption is on by default; it can be turned off with the daemon's
flag, but leaving it on is strongly recommended. A random nonce prefix per tunnel key, followed by a counter, prevents nonce reuse.

These mechanisms work together to make file transfer over Pilot as reliable as TCP while maintaining the NAT traversal properties of UDP. The sender and receiver code does not need to implement any of this -- it is handled by the Pilot daemon and driver library.
The trade-offs between using cloud storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) and direct Pilot transfer are significant across multiple dimensions:
1 direct hop when possible; relay adds a hop
No object-storage egress plan; relay transit may still carry infrastructure cost
No intermediate object copy; relay region may matter in fallback mode
TLS in transit, optional at rest
Relay, if used, sees ciphertext and connection metadata
No per-file cap in the streamed protocol; by default the receiver keeps at most 2 GiB of received files

The most compelling advantage of direct transfer is data privacy. When Agent A sends model weights directly to Agent B over a Pilot tunnel, no storage service holds a copy of the data. There is no S3 bucket to misconfigure, no IAM policy to audit, no cloud provider with access to stored objects. If the relay is used, it carries only ciphertext and connection metadata. That can make data-residency questions easier to answer, but it does not by itself make a system compliant with HIPAA, GDPR or any other regime.

The cost advantage also grows with scale. Cloud providers charge for data transferred out of object storage, and those fees add up for agents that move large checkpoints often. Direct transfer over Pilot has no object-storage fees -- the agents use their existing network connections.
Network interruptions are inevitable, especially for large file transfers. A dataset transfer that fails at 90% should not restart from zero.

For the hand-built protocol above, the implementation pattern is straightforward: the receiver tracks how many bytes it has written to disk. If the connection drops and the sender reconnects, the receiver sends the last received offset in its acceptance message, and the sender seeks to that position in the file before resuming:

The receiver can store the resume offset in a temporary metadata file alongside the partially received data. If the agent restarts entirely, it can detect the partial file, read the metadata, and request a resume from the sender. This makes large transfers resilient to transient network issues, daemon restarts, and even machine reboots.
Direct file transfer between agents unlocks several patterns that are impractical or expensive with cloud storage intermediaries:

A training agent produces a new model checkpoint and distributes it to inference agents across multiple regions. Each inference agent receives the weights directly, without the checkpoint ever landing in a shared bucket. This is faster (one hop instead of two) and more secure (no shared storage to compromise).
Two research agents working on related problems share preprocessed datasets directly. For more on this pattern, see
Secure Research Collaboration: Share Models, Not Data
. The key benefit is that data residency is maintained -- the dataset only exists on the two agents' machines, never in transit storage.

An analysis agent generates a PDF report and delivers it to a coordinator agent. The report may contain sensitive financial data that should not traverse cloud storage. Direct delivery ensures the report goes from producer to consumer with no intermediate copies.

Agents in a fleet share configuration files, prompt templates, or tool definitions. Instead of polling a central config server, agents push updates directly to peers. This eliminates the central config server as a single point of failure and reduces sync latency.
